newsitem.title: JAPAN: JGB squeeze spotlights issue of delivery failure.
newsitem.headline: JGB squeeze spotlights issue of delivery failure.

text.p: A severe squeeze in the Japanese government bond (JGB) market has sparked talk of the previously unthinkable -- allowing the failure of bond delivery -- in order to prevent a repetition of the problem.

The lack of a failure system was brought into focus by a squeeze by major U.S. brokerages last month in the cheapest cash JGBs deliverable against the September contract listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE).
The squeeze drove up the lending rate for the cheapest 161st 10-year JGB to a stunning 32 percent, traders said.
"A 32 percent repo rate is ridiculous. If failure was an option, it would never rise above a penalty rate as arbitrage mechanisms check such rises," said a bank trader.
An official with the TSE said that he was aware of the growing calls for a new mechanism to allow delivery failures, but also expressed caution over the launch of such a system.

"We're aware that a growing number of market participants are calling for a system allowing failures after the recent short-squeeze," said a department manager with the Clearing Administration at the TSE. "We will continue to get in touch with the market, while doing research of our own."
Banking authorities have showed concern over the recent squeeze, but are also hesitant to take any action.
"We're concerned if the reputation of the JGBs and liquidity thereof are damaged because the JGB market offers more chances for a squeeze," a Bank of Japan (BOJ) official said.
Other sources at the central bank said that the introduction of a failure system without strict rules could harm the stability of JGB transactions, reducing liquidity.
The JGB market is the world's second largest debt market after U.S. Treasuries.
Meanwhile, the BOJ is planning to introduce in 2000 a Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system in which payments are settled real-time instead of at the close of trading each day.
The RTGS system is already in operation in the United States, Britain and Switzerland.
Traders said the risk of being squeezed can also be reduced through stricter supervision by the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission and the TSE.
The September contract expired with a record open interest of 2.35 trillion yen, larger than the total amount of the cheapest deliverable JGBs available in the market.
Traders said that CS First Boston Ltd received about 1.8 trillion yen worth of the cash JGBs after having soaked up substantial deliverable cash issues from the market.
An official at the brokerage declined to comment.
Traders say growth of the repo market also holds the key.
At the moment, despite rising market turnover, participants in secured repo deals are still limited.
Public institutions with a large amount of JGBs on hand, such as the BOJ and the Trust Fund Bureau of the Ministry of Finance, have yet to join the repo market, traders said.
---Tokyo Treasury Desk 813-3432-8676
